summary: Presents an architecture for differentiated services on the Internet that uses two bits in the packet header, enough to offer a premium and an assured service. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two small marks on each packet tell routers how special it is. One mark means go quickly, the other means please try hard to deliver.

subtitle: Using two bits in the packet header to offer different service levels on the Internet.

tldr.problem: The Internet has historically offered only best-effort delivery, treating all traffic equally. As commercial services become important, some applications need guaranteed performance while others need only better-than-best-effort delivery.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes using two bits in the IP header (a Premium bit and an Assured bit) to mark packets for two service classes. Routers classify packets on these bits and serve Premium traffic at high priority and Assured traffic preferentially within a best-effort queue.
tldr.outcome: This architecture informed the later Differentiated Services (DiffServ) standards that became widely deployed. The simplicity of bit-marking at network edges rather than hop-by-hop reservation made differentiated services practical.

today: This RFC predates and informed RFC 2474 and RFC 2475, which standardized Differentiated Services (DiffServ). The two-bit concept evolved into the six-bit Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP), and the architecture—edge marking, core forwarding simplicity, and bilateral domain agreements—became the foundation of modern QoS on the Internet.

sections.title: The Need for Differentiated Services
sections.content:
The Internet currently delivers one type of service: best-effort delivery, where all traffic is treated equally. As the Internet became commercial, demand grew for guaranteed service quality for applications like voice-over-IP, video, and virtual private networks.

The challenge is providing different service levels without requiring the Internet's simple architecture to become complex. Rather than creating elaborate state at every router, this RFC proposes a simple solution: use a few bits in each packet's header to mark it for special treatment, with most complexity pushed to the network edges where there are fewer flows to manage.

The RFC uses an airline analogy: like first class, business class, and coach on planes, the Internet should support premium and assured services alongside best-effort, but best-effort should remain the dominant traffic type.
sections.eli5: The Internet treats all email and web traffic the same. But a video call should be faster and more reliable than a regular email. Two special bits in each packet can tell routers how to treat it.

sections.title: Premium Service: Guaranteed Performance
sections.content:
Premium service guarantees a specific peak bandwidth for a flow with minimal delay and no queue buildup. Think of it as a virtual leased line: a customer contracts for a peak rate, and the network promises that rate will be available.

Premium packets are shaped at the network edge to their contracted rate, with burst size limited to one or two packets. This shaping prevents bursty traffic from consuming link capacity unexpectedly. Inside the network, each router has two output queues—one for Premium packets, one for best-effort—and serves Premium first. Because Premium traffic is shaped to its peak rate and never oversubscribed, Premium queues remain small and never drop packets.

A customer might use Premium service to guarantee bandwidth for a critical business application, streaming video, or voice call. Since the network reserves capacity for Premium traffic, it must be priced accordingly. Unused Premium capacity can be allocated to best-effort traffic, so the network is not wasted when the premium customer is idle.
sections.eli5: Premium service is like buying a dedicated fast lane on the Internet. You pay for a certain speed, and the network guarantees you get it, like a telephone line.

sections.title: Assured Service: Better-Effort
sections.content:
Assured service provides traffic with better treatment than best-effort without the hard guarantees of Premium. Packets are statistically provisioned: the network commits to a typical usage profile, and traffic within that profile is treated preferentially when congestion occurs.

Unlike Premium, Assured traffic is not shaped at the edge; it can burst naturally. At each router, when a queue gets congested, the router uses RED (Random Early Detection) to drop unmarked best-effort packets before dropping Assured packets. This gives Assured traffic a lower drop probability, hence better likelihood of delivery, without limiting its rate rigidly.

Assured service is cheaper than Premium because it does not reserve capacity. A customer might purchase Assured service to make their web browsing or email feel more responsive during network congestion, but with the knowledge that some traffic may still be dropped during heavy congestion.
sections.eli5: Assured service is nicer than regular traffic but not as fast as Premium. If the network is busy, Assured packets get through before regular packets, but it is not a hard promise.

sections.title: Two-Bit Forwarding Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a simple two-bit marking scheme using the IP header precedence field. One bit marks Premium traffic (the P-bit), another marks Assured traffic (the A-bit). Both service types share simple forwarding mechanisms in routers.

At a leaf router (the first hop), packets are classified based on their source and destination addresses and ports. Matched flows have their bits set and are conditioned: Premium traffic is shaped through a token bucket, while Assured traffic is tested against a token bucket but not delayed if it exceeds the profile. Packets emerge with P or A bits set.

At each intermediate router, the only forwarding path action needed is to test the P-bit to choose between high-priority (Premium) and low-priority (best-effort plus Assured) queues. The low-priority queue applies RED queue management with two thresholds: one for best-effort traffic, one for Assured traffic, giving Assured packets preferential drop treatment.

At border routers between administrative domains, Profile Meters using token buckets check that traffic conforms to agreed-upon rates. Non-conformant Premium packets are dropped; non-conformant Assured packets are unmarked and treated as best-effort.
sections.eli5: Routers look at two special bits in each packet and decide which queue to put it in. Premium packets jump to the front, Assured packets skip ahead of regular traffic, and everything else goes in the regular queue.

sections.title: Bandwidth Brokers and Allocation
sections.content:
A Bandwidth Broker (BB) is an agent in each administrative domain that decides how to allocate Premium and Assured bandwidth to users and other domains. It maintains a policy database, authenticates requests, and configures leaf and border routers with traffic profiles.

The RFC envisions both static and dynamic allocation. Static allocation uses pre-negotiated contracts: an ISP and customer agree in advance on the bandwidth the customer may use, configured into routers at the start of the service period. Dynamic allocation allows requests during the service period, with Bandwidth Brokers from adjacent domains negotiating in real time to reserve bandwidth across domain boundaries.

Bilateral agreements between adjacent domain Bandwidth Brokers replace the need for complex multilateral negotiations. Each domain controls allocation within itself, and agreements at boundaries determine how much marked traffic can flow between domains. This architecture scales to the entire Internet by following existing administrative hierarchies and routing paths.
sections.eli5: A bandwidth broker is like a traffic manager for each network. It decides who gets to use the fast Premium and Assured lanes, and it talks to other network managers about how much traffic can cross their borders.

left.title: Premium Service
left.desc: Guaranteed rate, shaped traffic, minimal queue, no drops, high cost.

right.title: Assured Service
right.desc: Statistical guarantee, unshaped traffic, lower drop probability, lower cost.
